intro.rule1: Nothing is urgent. Bitcoin cannot be stolen by waiting. It can be lost by rushing.

days.title: Secure the paper, touch nothing
notes: Rule #1 outranks everything: nothing is urgent — Bitcoin cannot be stolen by waiting but can be lost by rushing.
Read the day once today, do only Day 1, and come back tomorrow.
How you should feel after today: organized — nothing is lost, nothing is at risk, and that is a full day's work.
days.feel_after: Organized. Nothing is lost. Nothing is at risk. That is a full day's work.
dos: Collect everything Bitcoin-related into one box you control:
Any hardware wallets, USB sticks, cards with a chip (Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Trezor, Coldcard, Bitkey)
Any papers with handwritten or printed lists of words (12 or 24, or numbered groups — sometimes split across pages)
Any "wallet files", USB drives labeled with wallet names, letters of instruction, envelopes with instructions
Anything metal with words/letters stamped or punched into it
Keep the box somewhere safe and normal (a lockable drawer, a safe).
Write down (on paper, not in the app) where you found each thing.
donts: Do not plug anything in yet.
Do not reset, format, "clean up", or wipe any device — even if it seems locked or broken.
Do not photograph word lists. Phones automatically back up photos to the cloud, and a photo of a seed phrase is a permanent leak.
Do not type the words into any app, website, or this app.
Do not delete anything on his computer or phone — "wallet" files, "Ledger Live", "Sparrow", "Electrum" — nothing.
Do not tell anyone what you found or how much there is.

days.title: Make a written inventory (no secrets on the page)
notes: The inventory records what each thing is and where it was found, never the secrets on it.
Exchange statements and tax mail are records, not keys, so they are fine to read and keep.
dos: For each item in the box, write one line:
What it physically is ("small black device, buttons, 'Ledger' on back")
Where it was found ("second drawer of his desk")
Anything written on it or its packaging ("label says 'main'")
Also walk the house for things that aren't in the box yet:
Safe deposit box? Home safe? Attorney's office? Bank vault?
A laptop he used alone (check browser bookmarks later — Day 4)
An app on his phone: "Sparrow", "BlueWallet", "Muun", "Nunchuk", "River", "Strike", "Cash App", "Coinbase" — list the names, open nothing yet.
Today you may also check: any mail/emails about Bitcoin tax forms, statements, or exchange accounts. List the company names you see. These are records, not keys — they are fine to read and keep.
donts: Do not copy the words into your inventory — write only: "24-word list found, sealed envelope, 3 pages."

days.title: Learn what each thing is (the app explains, the box stays closed)
notes: You are building just enough understanding to make Day 4 and Day 5 safe.
dos: Open the app's Learn mode and read the short guides for whatever Day 2 found. Typical reading for an heir:
"What is a seed phrase?" (5 min)
"What is a hardware wallet?" (5 min)
"What is Sparrow / Ledger Live / an exchange account?" (5 min each)
"What is multisig? What is a 'descriptor' file?" (10 min — only if you found 2+ hardware wallets or a file mentioning '2 of 3')
If any sentence confuses you, ask the app to re-explain it simpler. That is exactly what it is for.

days.title: Look, don't touch (verification with open eyes)
notes: Today you are answering: is this a device-and-words setup, one with an extra passphrase, a multisig setup with several devices, and/or accounts at companies — most setups are one of those four shapes.
Word-completeness checks (24 vs 12 words, split pages, SLIP-39 numbered groups) are done on paper, never by typing the words.
dos: Exchange accounts (River, Strike, Swan, Coinbase…): you can see whether an account exists without touching funds.
confirm each list is complete (the number of words it claims — usually 24)
note their brand and model from the packaging or the back of the device
open his browser bookmarks. Wallet-related bookmarks are safe to look at
donts: Do not log into anything; just note the names.
Do not power them on yet
Do not try to reset passwords today — account recovery is a legal/identity process you will do deliberately in Day 5–6 with documents in hand

days.title: Know your options (no action yet)
notes: Path A is the heirs' default and the money never passes through anyone's hands.
Custodial exchanges can freeze accounts during compliance reviews, and nothing there is "yours" in the self-custody sense.
Path C calls for a Bitcoin-knowledgeable estate attorney, not a "recovery expert".
The app never picks a paid professional for you.
dos: Path A — Keep it in self-custody (heirs' default): The keys already work; nothing needs to move. In the coming weeks you will learn to open the wallet on a clean computer, verify you can see the balance (watch-only first), and only then decide anything. Slow, safe, and the money never passes through anyone's hands.

Path B — Move to a temporary custodian while you decide: Some heirs want funds somewhere simpler while the estate is sorted. If you go this way, the corpus directory names Bitcoin-only companies with strong customer service, proof of reserves, and long track records — and states their criticisms honestly (custodial exchanges can freeze accounts during compliance reviews; nothing there is "yours" in the self-custody sense).

Path C — Get professional help for complex estates: Large amounts, multiple keys with missing pieces, business entities, or any legal complication → a Bitcoin-knowledgeable estate attorney (not a "recovery expert") and possibly a collaborative-custody provider with a documented inheritance process. The directory lists categories and evidence; the app never picks a paid professional for you.
The app has deep-dive guides for each.
donts: Moving funds means the keys were used, so this is only done once you have practiced recovering the wallet yourself. Never because a stranger suggested it.

days.title: Assemble your verification plan
notes: The first real action is always the same: prove you can open the wallet without risking anything.
The verification sequence is the single most safety-critical step in the walkthrough and should be done in one sitting.
Enter the seed words once, and only into verified software.
dos: A clean computer (his old laptop, wiped/reinstalled, or your own device used offline) — the app's guide explains what "clean" means and why.
The wallet software — downloaded only from the official site, with the checksum verification the guide walks you through (this is where the app earns its keep — verification is mechanical and safe).

The order of operations — the non-negotiable sequence: 1. Install software → 2. Verify download → 3. Enter the seed words ONCE (into the verified software only) → 4. Write down the first receiving address → 5. Confirm the balance appears (or ask the app why it doesn't) → 6. Nothing else.
A helper rule: one difficult thing per day.
donts: No sending, no "upgrading", no swapping wallets the same day.
Two in one day is how mistakes happen.

days.title: Rest, then repeat what worked
notes: If you completed Day 6's verification and saw the balance, you have already done the hardest part.
It was done without spending anything, without sharing anything, and without trusting anyone.
Rule #1 still applies: nothing is urgent and every safe step can be taken calmly.
dos: Re-read your inventory and your Day 6 plan.
Start the next phase at your pace: the app's guides on "spending safely", "moving to your own custody", "tax basics", and the directory are there when you're ready.
